title: Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation
mission: Ensure meal-level protein supply delivers the amino-acid foundation neurotransmitter pathways depend on.
summary: Food protein supplies indispensable amino acids—the amino acids the body cannot make in sufficient amounts—including phenylalanine and tryptophan. Phenylalanine can also be converted to tyrosine. After a protein meal, dietary phenylalanine appears in the circulation. Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later signalling can use for dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. Protein that covers those amino acids is the supported dietary route.
dose_sensitivity: Not established as a neurotransmitter dose. Protein type, dose and age change how much dietary phenylalanine reaches the circulation. Extra protein is not shown to raise brain monoamines.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Coverage of the indispensable amino-acid set, including phenylalanine, that sets the circulating pool neurotransmitter pathways can draw on. Meals contribute measurable amino-acid composition; this is not a requirement that each meal provide complete coverage
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Protein-quality scoring and vegetarian-diet amino-acid coverage do not establish that increasing protein raises brain monoamine synthesis or improves attention or mood. The indispensable set includes phenylalanine; tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted precursor/transport role, but this entry does not explicitly establish its dietary supply route. Clarification required; not defaulted to No.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Catecholamine precursor in the circulating pool this PM prioritises. Tyrosine is normally formed from indispensable phenylalanine and can become conditionally indispensable when phenylalanine availability is limited
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid. Pool presence or dietary tyrosine is not evidence for increased brain dopamine or noradrenaline, LAT1 advantage, or clinical benefit. Absence of a phenylalanine atom is an evidence-scope decision, not a claim that phenylalanine is absent from the indispensable pool.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.

dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Pool presence of tryptophan is not evidence for increased brain serotonin, brain entry, or an attention or mood benefit.

dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Protein-quality scoring and vegetarian-diet amino-acid coverage do not establish that increasing protein raises brain monoamine synthesis or improves attention or mood. The indispensable set includes phenylalanine; tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Tyrosine is a catecholamine-precursor substrate in the pool this PM prioritises. It is normally formed from phenylalanine and is not classified as an indispensable amino acid.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid. Pool presence or dietary tyrosine is not evidence for increased brain dopamine or noradrenaline, LAT1 advantage, or clinical benefit. Absence of a phenylalanine atom is an evidence-scope decision, not a claim that phenylalanine is absent from the indispensable pool.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Tryptophan is an indispensable Direct substrate in the pool this PM governs. Presence in meals is not a serotonin-dosing rule.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Pool presence of tryptophan is not evidence for increased brain serotonin, brain entry, or an attention or mood benefit.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: Imbalance of LAT1 competitive large-neutral-amino-acid balance can constrain this mechanism’s governed circulating amino-acid pool.
established_links: This mechanism’s overview treats circulating pool sufficiency as independent of blood–brain-barrier transport.
Fernstrom 2013 locates LNAA competition at LAT1, which is the transport mechanism.
inferred_links: LAT1 imbalance would therefore reduce the circulating pool this PM governs.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: The named competitive state is brain-entry competition, not circulating-pool availability. That is a different process. Neither assessed arm is admitted as a mapping to the current KC1 definition.

kc_change_control_flags.proposition: Candidate PM↔KC1 mapping on the amino-acid quality arm. Shared IAA/protein-quality pool may constrain this PM; competitive LAT1 balance is not this PM's relationship. Input overlap with §4.1.1 is not a rejection criterion. Public §4.1.3 has no mapping. Dual-arm iKC remains KC-owned.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Meal protein supplies circulating phenylalanine, and phenylalanine can be converted to tyrosine. Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later catecholamine and serotonin pathways can use. These studies do not measure attention.
Phenylalanine from dietary protein can be converted to tyrosine, the dopamine precursor. That supply is not a measurement of motivation or drive, and it is not dopaminergic signalling.
Tryptophan is an indispensable amino acid and the serotonin precursor. Coverage of that amino acid is not a measurement of emotional regulation, and serotonin signalling is a later step.

scientific_findings_intro: Dietary protein supplies the circulating precursor pool; food structure and source can alter delivery kinetics without proving superior neurotransmitter function. Curated reaction identity, whole-diet adequacy and experimental intervention findings are distinguished below.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Dietary protein delivers circulating phenylalanine; kinetics depend on context
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Human tracer studies establish dietary delivery. Cross-study source/dose comparisons and variable age results require qualified interpretation.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Dietary protein supplies phenylalanine to the human circulation, with delivery kinetics varying by the tested protein source, dose and meal context. The pooled age association is context-dependent, not proof that ageing uniformly impairs absorption or that greater availability increases brain neurotransmitters.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The pooled dairy corpus establishes dietary tracer appearance but is not 18 independent research-group replications. Independent human source comparisons support context-dependent plasma responses. An individual exercise study and the newer six-source crossover did not show a uniform age-related decrement; plasma profiles and dietary tracer appearance are not identical measurements.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Mostly male dairy-tracer cohorts; between-study source/dose contrasts, nonrandomised age comparisons and different matrices limit generalisation. No brain transport, neurotransmitter or ADHD endpoint.

evidence_considered.label: Gorissen et al. (2020)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary whey, casein or milk protein
evidence_considered.directional_finding: About half of dietary protein-derived phenylalanine appeared in the circulation over five hours. The fraction was lower for casein, higher with a larger dose, and slightly lower in older adults.

assessment.study: Pooled analysis of 18 randomised trials using intrinsically labelled whey, casein or milk protein.
assessment.population: 602 participants, mean age 53 years. The age comparison used 82 young adults and 83 older adults.
assessment.result: Dietary phenylalanine entered the circulation. Protein type, dose and age changed the fraction that appeared.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Mean appearance 50% ± 14% over five hours. Casein 45% ± 11%, whey 57% ± 10%, milk 65% ± 13%. Older adults 45% ± 10% versus young adults 51% ± 14%.
assessment.evidence_summary: A protein meal delivers phenylalanine into the circulation, and the amount depends on the protein, the dose and age.
assessment.limitations: Phenylalanine appearance is not the full indispensable set, not tryptophan, and not a brain or clinical endpoint.

evidence_considered.label: Non-animal protein-source crossover (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 30 g protein as milk, mycoprotein, pea, lupin, spirulina or chlorella; five-hour sampling; at least seven-day washout.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.

assessment.study: Independent Exeter programme; randomised double-blind six-period crossover, 12 young and 10 older adults, both sexes.
assessment.population: Independent Exeter programme; randomised double-blind six-period crossover, 12 young and 10 older adults, both sexes.
assessment.result: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Source-specific endpoint and uncertainty: Small cohorts; composition and food matrix differ, so no isolated digestibility estimate or universal ranking follows.
assessment.evidence_summary: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.
assessment.limitations: Small cohorts; composition and food matrix differ, so no isolated digestibility estimate or universal ranking follows. Independent of Maastricht pooled dairy corpus; age analyses and six visits within a person are not six independent replications.

evidence_considered.label: Pennings et al. (2011): exercise before protein
evidence_considered.exposure_context: Resistance-type exercise before labelled protein versus rest; six-hour tracer follow-up.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.

assessment.study: Young/older men, rest/exercise comparisons; 48 participants total.
assessment.population: Young/older men, rest/exercise comparisons; 48 participants total.
assessment.result: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Source-specific endpoint and uncertainty: Muscle utilisation is not circulating-pool enhancement; a nonsignificant contrast is not equivalence.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.
assessment.limitations: Muscle utilisation is not circulating-pool enhancement; a nonsignificant contrast is not equivalence. NCT00557388 is part of Gorissen2020; no double-counting.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Diet-wide amino-acid adequacy does not require identical complete meals
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Retain nutritional adequacy, but separate whole-diet coverage from acute food-specific kinetics.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Varied adult diets can provide digestible indispensable amino acids without requiring every meal to supply the full set. This nutritional-adequacy proposition does not establish an optimal neurotransmitter dose or demonstrate that all plant and animal foods have identical postprandial responses.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Existing vegetarian-diet and DIAAS reviews support adequacy across a varied diet. New human source and faba-bean studies qualify single-food composition/digestibility; they do not contradict adequate mixed diets. The recent systematic requirement review concerns quantitative requirements, not neurotransmitter enhancement.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Requirement reviews are not direct tests of neurotransmitter response or every possible plant diet. Energy sufficiency, variety, age and clinical context remain relevant.

evidence_considered.label: Mariotti and Gardner (2019)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Adult vegetarian diets that include protein-rich plant foods can meet protein and amino-acid requirements. Amino-acid deficiency is described as overstated.

assessment.study: Review of protein and amino-acid intakes from vegetarian and vegan diets in Western adults.
assessment.population: Adults, including older adults, eating vegetarian or vegan diets. Children are discussed separately.
assessment.result: Protein-rich plant foods can achieve protein and amino-acid adequacy in adults.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No single intake-response estimate. The result is adequacy against requirements, not a change in brain transmitters.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary patterns can cover the indispensable amino acids this pool requires.
assessment.limitations: Requirement coverage is not a plasma time course and not a neurotransmitter outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Moughan and Lim (2024)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Protein quality is scored by digestible indispensable amino acids rather than by protein grams alone.

assessment.study: Review of the digestible indispensable amino acid score a decade after its introduction.
assessment.population: Not a new human trial. The score is applied to foods and diets.
assessment.result: Quality depends on digestible indispensable amino acids.
assessment.evidence_summary: Coverage of those amino acids is the quality claim this mechanism can use.
assessment.limitations: A scoring review does not measure circulating or brain amino acids.

evidence_considered.label: Marsh et al. (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Varied plant-protein sources across the diet can cover indispensable amino acids without combining complementary proteins in each meal.

assessment.study: Review of protein in vegetarian diets.
assessment.result: Completeness can be reached across the day rather than inside every meal.
assessment.evidence_summary: Each meal does not have to supply the full indispensable set.
assessment.limitations: The review does not test brain precursor availability.

scientific_findings.finding_summary: Established conversion chemistry; dietary admission and downstream catecholamine effects remain separate decisions.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Phenylalanine-4-hydroxylase (PAH) converts L-phenylalanine to L-tyrosine. This endogenous route contributes to tyrosine supply but does not make tyrosine absent from foods or establish an independent requirement for extra dietary tyrosine.
scientific_findings.synthesis: UniProt P00439 and Rhea 20273 establish reaction identity; the Matthews human kinetic review remains linked for physiological context. No new intake-response or clinical conclusion is inferred.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Curated enzyme annotation does not quantify whole-body dietary contribution or human brain catecholamine flux. Do not automatically add every PAH cofactor as a PM1-specific dietary requirement.

evidence_considered.label: Matthews (2007)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine in humans. Tyrosine is normally dispensable and can become conditionally indispensable when phenylalanine availability is limited.

assessment.study: Overview of human phenylalanine and tyrosine tracer kinetics.
assessment.population: Human tracer studies in people with ordinary hydroxylation and in disorders that block it.
assessment.result: Phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine. The conversion depends on phenylalanine availability.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Kinetic rates are reviewed. No dietary dose for a brain catecholamine change is given.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary phenylalanine can supply tyrosine through a conversion that has been measured in humans.
assessment.limitations: Conversion kinetics are not brain dopamine or noradrenaline synthesis.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Downstream precursor identity is not a dietary efficacy result
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Preserve precursor identity and the downstream PM2-PM5 boundary.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Tyrosine and tryptophan supply the precursor pathways for catecholamines and serotonin, respectively. Their biochemical identity does not demonstrate that additional meal protein improves brain transmitter synthesis, attention, mood or reward.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Retain Aquili and existing precursor evidence as biochemical/contextual support, not evidence that ordinary dietary coverage reproduces depletion or pharmacological supplementation experiments.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Transport competition, regional synthesis, release and clinical outcomes require their own evidence. No score is inherited from this elementary relationship.

evidence_considered.label: Aquili (2020)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: narrative review of depletion and supplementation studies
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Tryptophan is named as the serotonin precursor and tyrosine as the dopamine precursor. The reviewed behavioural effects come from depletion and supplementation, not from meal-protein coverage.

assessment.study: Narrative review of tryptophan and tyrosine in executive function and reward.
assessment.population: The behavioural studies are mostly acute depletion or supplementation experiments.
assessment.result: The precursor relationship is stated. Cognitive effects in the review are not effects of this dietary pool.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No effect size for meal protein on brain transmitters.
assessment.evidence_summary: The precursor names are supported. The cognitive conclusions are not a result for this mechanism.
assessment.limitations: Depletion and isolated supplements are not indispensable-amino-acid coverage.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Mincing changed dietary phenylalanine appearance in older men
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In a randomised crossover study of ten older men, 135 g minced beef produced greater six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance than the same quantity of steak. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle protein synthesis did not differ detectably between preparations.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Texture affected source-specific tracer delivery, not every circulating or functional outcome.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The matched-food crossover supports a preparation effect on dietary tracer appearance. Null total-concentration and muscle outcomes prevent a generic better-protein or neurotransmitter interpretation. The thesis and publication describe one dataset.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: One small older-male trial; no independent replication of the exact matched-beef protocol was established in this assessment. No claim that all foods should be minced or that this improves attention.

evidence_considered.label: Pennings et al. (2013): minced beef versus steak
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 135 g intrinsically labelled lean beef, same cut, minced patty versus steak; six-hour tracer follow-up.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.

assessment.study: Randomised crossover; ten older men, mean age 74 years; two visits at least 14 days apart.
assessment.population: Randomised crossover; ten older men, mean age 74 years; two visits at least 14 days apart.
assessment.result: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance: minced 61% ± 3% versus steak 49% ± 3% (means ± SEM), P < 0.01; 12 percentage-point difference. No paired confidence interval calculated or inferred.
assessment.evidence_summary: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.
assessment.limitations: Small single trial; mean estimates and standard errors available, paired effect interval not extracted; no equivalence claim for null outcomes. Single empirical dataset; thesis and journal article are the same experiment, not replications.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Extrusion altered early amino-acid kinetics, not demonstrated total loss
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In a randomised crossover of nine healthy young adults, the tested high-moisture-extruded mycoprotein/pea blend delayed selected early plasma amino-acid responses relative to the dry blend. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different; the study does not establish poorer overall nutrition for all meat alternatives.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Preserve both temporal differences and the null integrated endpoint.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The human beverage experiment and in-vitro analyses address different endpoints. Selected phenylalanine/tyrosine peaks changed, while grouped integrated responses were statistically inconclusive. Composition, matrix and sampling constrain interpretation.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Single small trial, no dietary tracer, numerous secondary endpoints and laboratory reconstituted products. Not proof of equal total absorption or a reason to avoid all processed plant foods.

evidence_considered.label: High-moisture extrusion crossover (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 25 g protein, 39% mycoprotein/61% pea; extruded versus dry-milled blend in drinks; five-hour samples.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Extrusion delayed early responses and reduced selected peaks, including phenylalanine and tyrosine. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different.

assessment.study: Randomised double-blind counterbalanced crossover; nine young adults, five men/four women; minimum five-day separation.
assessment.population: Randomised double-blind counterbalanced crossover; nine young adults, five men/four women; minimum five-day separation.
assessment.result: Extrusion delayed early responses and reduced selected peaks, including phenylalanine and tyrosine. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Phenylalanine peak: dry blend 72 ± 3 versus extruded 58 ± 3 micromol/L, P=0.020; time to peak 32 ± 4 versus 83 ± 20 minutes, P=0.037 (means ± SEM). Total five-hour grouped amino-acid iAUC: no statistically significant difference; no equivalence bounds inferred.
assessment.evidence_summary: Extrusion delayed early responses and reduced selected peaks, including phenylalanine and tyrosine. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different.
assessment.limitations: Small single dataset; no tracer, many endpoints, uncertainty on paired differences; laboratory reconstituted products not every commercial meat alternative. Distinct study but same Exeter programme as nonanimal2024; not an independent replication of its six-source comparison.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

decision.applicability_proposition: This mechanism governs the shared indispensable-amino-acid quality and availability pool.
established_links: Meal-level protein quantity, quality and distribution set the circulating indispensable-amino-acid pool this PM governs (PM1 mission and overview).
Mariotti 2019 and Moughan/DIAAS-type scoring describe IAA adequacy of that pool.
inferred_links: Incomplete pool quality would also raise brain monoamines or treat ADHD.
decision.rationale: Reassessed after user review: indispensable-amino-acid provision is already recorded in PM1-DIT-1 and does not establish an additional constraint. The canonical KC1 defines monoamine-precursor LNAA competitive transport, which is outside this PM's circulating-pool provision boundary. The prior quality-arm admission used the historical KC scope and is superseded; its evidence remains on the dietary atoms and this assessment.

kc_adjudication_history.rationale: Superseded scope: this proposition concerns the former broad indispensable-amino-acid quality arm. Current BRS1 KC1 is the monoamine-precursor LNAA competitive pool. Archiving does not reject general protein-quality biology or alter the separately assessed competitive/supply decisions.

evidence_qualification.label: Diet-Dominant
evidence_qualification.rationale: Retain the Diet-Dominant qualification for experimentally demonstrated dietary precursor provision, without a superiority claim.
evidence_qualification.scope_note: Human dietary tracer appearance and source-specific plasma profiles are not brain neurotransmitter or ADHD outcomes.

routes.intervention_effect: Dietary protein ingestion delivers labelled phenylalanine, with source and dose contrasts in human studies.
routes.context: Human controlled feeding/tracer experiments; mainly healthy adults.
routes.limitations: Meal source, dose, age and matrix constrain generalisation; adequacy is not enhancement.

routes.intervention_effect: Matched mincing-versus-steak changed six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance.
routes.context: Ten older men; same-cut beef crossover.
routes.limitations: One small older-male trial; no independent replication of the exact matched-beef protocol was established in this assessment. No claim that all foods should be minced or that this improves attention.

principal_route_selection.rationale: Dietary Requirements remains the principal supply route: feeding interventions directly deliver the indispensable precursor pool across relevant protein sources. The selected preparation SOP addresses a narrower older-male context, not a replacement for dietary provision.
principal_route_selection.comparative_limitations: No head-to-head superiority over all lifestyle or optimisation routes is established. Prominence concerns the mission-specific supply process; it is not a nutrient-benefit ranking.

assessments.relevance: The PM mission is dietary delivery to the circulating amino-acid pool.
assessments.directness: Human labelled dietary-protein experiments measure this supply rather than infer it from food content.
assessments.extent: Repeated feeding experiments show substantial dietary tracer appearance, qualified by five/six-hour windows, source, dose and population. No universal optimum or brain effect.
